class FleaPlans(models.TextChoices):
    #  __new__ must come BEFORE the member declarations
    def __new__(cls, value, desc, label):
        obj = str.__new__(cls, value)   # value is what gets stored in the DB
        obj._value_ = value
        obj._label_ = label             # label is what Django shows in forms/admin
        obj.desc = desc                 # your custom extra field
        return obj

    # tuple order must match (value, desc, label)

Q: svn checkout fails with "E160006: No such revision" after relocation and upgrade A:

So I figured out a solution to this problem myself. Because I had the original, uncorrupted repository around, I created a new clone of that using:

svnadmin create /path/to/newclone
svnsync initialize file:///path/to/newclone https://url/to/orginalrepo
svnsync sync file:///path/to/newclone

Then I instructed that new clone to sync to the old (corrupted) clone of the original repo:

svnsync initialize --allow-non-empty file:///path/to/newclone file:///path/to/oldclone

The --allow-non-empty option allowed me to sync recent revisions in oldclone, without worrying about the fact that there are revisions in newclone that are absent from oldclone:

svnsync sync file:///path/to/newclone

This produced a working repository with all the revisions from both originalrepo and oldclone.

Q: Java - Deleting previous console inputs out of System.in - Why does 1 version of my Code work and not the other version? A:

Why Version 1 fails to empty the stream:

When you type 1, 2, 3, and 4 followed by enters, all those bytes are sent to the System.in buffer.

  • On the very first iteration of the while loop in Version 1, you call scanner.nextLine().

  • Instead of reading just a single line from System.in, your static scanner reads ahead and pulls ALL available data from System.in into its own large internal memory buffer to optimize performance.

  • Because the data was moved from System.in to the scanner buffer, System.in.available() immediately drops to 0.

  • The loop breaks right away after consuming only the first line (1), leaving 2, 3, and 4 safely stored inside the static scanner instance. When you call scanner.nextLine() in your main method, it just grabs what was already fetched.

Why Version 2 works:

In Version 2, every single loop iteration initializes a brand new Scanner wrapper object (new Scanner(System.in)).

  • The first dummyScanner grabs everything available in System.in, consumes the first line, and gets thrown away when the block scope ends.

  • However, unlike Version 1, any residual data left in that dummy scanner's internal buffer is permanently lost and discarded along with the object.

  • As long as there is still raw data left untouched in the terminal link, System.in.available() evaluates to greater than 0 again on the next cycle, a new dummy scanner consumes another portion, and the process repeats until the stream is cleared.

A cleaner, non-looping alternative to flush System.in:

Creating multiple scanners per loop can cause structural issues or lock inputs in real projects. If you want to reliably clear any pending data directly from the stream before reading new console entries, you can use System.in.skip() using the bytes available:

Java

private static void deleteInput() {
    try {
        int availableBytes = System.in.available();
        if (availableBytes > 0) {
            System.in.skip(availableBytes);
        }
    } catch (IOException e) {
        e.printStackTrace();
    }
}

Note: Make sure to invoke this before creating or using the final Scanner that will expect the fresh inputs, as an already instantiated Scanner might still hold pre-fetched chunks.
